analogy.p: Think of A as what you see on the screen of a map app and n as the zoom level. The picture A (between 1 and 10) is always roughly the same size on your screen, but the zoom level n tells you whether you are looking at a street (10^-3 km) or at a continent (10^3 km). Moving one zoom step changes the scale by exactly a factor of 10, which is what increasing n by 1 does. The analogy breaks down because real map zoom levels are not exact factors of ten and A is not just a picture: in standard form, changing n without compensating by changing A changes the actual value of the number.
analogy.t: The zoom level on a map

bullets: Standard form is also called **scientific notation**; the two names mean exactly the same thing.
Large numbers have a **positive** power of 10, for example 3 000 000 = 3 × 10^6.
Small numbers (between 0 and 1) have a **negative** power of 10, for example 0.000 04 = 4 × 10^-5.
Numbers from 1 up to (but not including) 10 have a power of **0**, for example 7.2 = 7.2 × 10^0, because 10^0 = 1.
The power n tells you the **size (order of magnitude)** of the number, so comparing two standard form numbers is quick.
It is used heavily in GCSE science (physics, chemistry and biology) as well as maths, so fluency here also earns marks in other subjects.
core.h: What standard form is and why we use it
core.p: **Standard form** is a way of writing very large or very small numbers compactly, as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10. The specification asks you to **calculate with and interpret numbers in the form A × 10^n, where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer**, including converting between ordinary numbers and standard form, comparing and ordering them, and doing calculations with them, with and without a calculator. It is the standard way scientists record things like the distance to the Sun (about 1.5 × 10^8 km) or the mass of an electron (about 9.11 × 10^-31 kg), because writing all the zeros would be slow and error-prone.

bullets: A × 10^n with **1 ≤ A < 10** (A can equal 1 but can never equal 10) and **n an integer**.
**Not** standard form: 45 × 10^6 (A is 45, too big), 0.45 × 10^8 (A is 0.45, too small), 10 × 10^3 (A is 10), 3.2 × 10^1.5 (power not an integer).
A single digit counts: 3 × 10^4 is standard form with A = 3.
The decimal point in A goes **after the first non-zero digit**.
Be careful with the 'times' sign: it is × (multiply), not an x or a letter, and the power is written above and to the right of the 10.
Quick test: 'Is A between 1 and 10 and is the power a whole number?' If both answers are yes, it is standard form.
core.p: A number is in standard form only if it satisfies **two** conditions: the first part, A, is at least 1 but less than 10, and the second part is 10 raised to an **integer** power n (positive, negative or zero). A is often a decimal, such as 4.5 or 1.28, and can have as many digits as the accuracy requires. The strict test is on the first part: it must have **exactly one non-zero digit before the decimal point**. If that is not true, the number is not in standard form, even though its value may be correct.

bullets: Step 1: find the first non-zero digit and put the decimal point just after it, giving A.
Step 2: count how many places the decimal point moved to the left. This is n.
Step 3: write A × 10^n with n positive.
Example: 45 000 000 → 4.5 (the point moved 7 places left) → 4.5 × 10^7.
Trailing zeros after the last non-zero digit are not written in A, unless they are significant, so 3 600 000 = 3.6 × 10^6.
Check: n is always one less than the number of digits in a whole number, for example 4 500 000 has 7 digits so n = 6.
Words: 1 thousand = 10^3, 1 million = 10^6, 1 billion = 10^9 (a thousand million), so 2.5 billion = 2.5 × 10^9.
core.h: Writing large numbers in standard form
core.p: To write a large number in standard form, imagine moving the decimal point until there is exactly one non-zero digit in front of it. The number of places you move the point is the power n, and because the number was big, n is **positive**. The reason this works is that each move of the decimal point one place to the left divides the number by 10, so to keep the value the same we must multiply by 10 once for each move. Remember that a whole number has its decimal point at the end, even though it is not written.

bullets: Step 1: put the decimal point after the first non-zero digit to get A.
Step 2: count the places moved to the right; call this k.
Step 3: write A × 10^-k.
Example: 0.00032 → 3.2 (point moved 4 places right) → 3.2 × 10^-4.
The number of places moved is **not** the number of zeros after the decimal point: 0.00032 has three zeros but n = -4. A reliable rule is 'the position of the first non-zero digit after the point'.
A negative power does **not** mean a negative number. 3.2 × 10^-4 is positive (0.00032).
Negative numbers can also be in standard form, for example -4.5 × 10^6; the minus sign goes in front of A.
core.h: Writing small numbers in standard form
core.p: To write a number between 0 and 1 in standard form, move the decimal point to the **right** until it is after the first non-zero digit. The number of moves is the size of the power, and because the original number was small, n is **negative**. Each move to the right multiplies the number by 10, so to keep the value the same we must divide by 10 each time, which is the same as multiplying by 10^-1. The most common error is miscounting the places, so count carefully, including the zero in front of the decimal point.

bullets: Positive n: move the point n places to the right. 3.5 × 10^4 = 35 000.
Positive n with more places than digits: 6.2 × 10^5 = 620 000 (add zeros).
Negative n: move the point |n| places to the left. 7.2 × 10^-3 = 0.0072.
2.05 × 10^-2 = 0.0205 (the zero between 2 and 5 stays).
Sense check: a **big** n (positive) means a **big** number; a **negative** n means a number **smaller than 1**.
If the answer needs to be in decimal form, write it with the decimal point in the right place and zeros as placeholders, not with spaces missing.
core.h: Converting standard form back to an ordinary number
core.p: To convert A × 10^n back to an ordinary number, move the decimal point of A by n places: **right** if n is positive and **left** if n is negative. Fill the gaps with zeros as needed. This reverses the earlier methods, and it is a good way to check your answers: always check that a number written in standard form looks the right size when converted back.

bullets: 10^0 = 1, because any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1.
Prefixes: kilo = 10^3, mega = 10^6, giga = 10^9; milli = 10^-3, micro = 10^-6, nano = 10^-9. So 5 nm = 5 × 10^-9 m.
A million is 10^6, a billion is 10^9, a trillion is 10^12.
Learning these few results means you can do most standard form conversions in your head.
core.p: Standard form depends on a solid understanding of powers of 10. A power of 10 is a 1 followed by zeros (for positive powers) or a decimal with a 1 in a particular place (for negative powers). The rules of indices explain why the system works: multiplying by 10^n shifts digits n places to the left, while 10^-n divides by 10^n and shifts digits n places to the right. This understanding also helps with the multiplication and division of standard form numbers.

bullets: Larger power wins: 2 × 10^7 > 9 × 10^6, even though 9 > 2.
Equal powers: compare the A parts, so 4.2 × 10^-3 < 4.7 × 10^-3.
Negative powers: -2 is bigger than -3, so 5 × 10^-2 (0.05) > 5 × 10^-3 (0.005). Watch this one!
To order a list: write all numbers in standard form, order by n (largest first or smallest first), then by A for ties.
To find how many times bigger one number is, divide them (see later).
Convert to ordinary numbers if asked to prove which is bigger, but standard form is quicker and clearer.
core.h: Ordering and comparing numbers in standard form
core.p: To compare numbers in standard form, always compare the **powers of 10 first**; the number with the larger power is bigger, as long as both numbers are in proper standard form. Only if the powers are equal do you compare the A values. This works because the power tells you the order of magnitude, while A only changes the number by less than a factor of ten. If a number is not yet in standard form, convert it first.

bullets: Step 1: multiply the A parts using a calculator if allowed.
Step 2: add the powers of 10.
Step 3: check that the A part is between 1 and 10; if not, adjust.
Example: (3.2 × 10^5) × (4 × 10^3) = 12.8 × 10^8. A = 12.8 is too big, so move the point one place left and add 1 to the power: 1.28 × 10^9.
Direction of adjusting: if A is **too big** (10 or more), divide A by 10 and **add 1** to n. If A is **too small** (below 1), multiply A by 10 and **subtract 1** from n.
Always show the intermediate line (like 12.8 × 10^8) because it earns a method mark.
core.p: To multiply two numbers in standard form, **multiply the A parts** and **add the powers of 10**. The rule follows from the laws of indices: (A × 10^m) × (B × 10^n) = (A × B) × 10^(m+n), because multiplication can be done in any order. The answer must then be checked: if A × B is 10 or more, or less than 1, you must adjust it and change the power to restore standard form. This adjustment step is often the last mark in the question.

bullets: Step 1: divide the A parts.
Step 2: subtract the second power from the first.
Step 3: check A and adjust if necessary.
Example: (2.4 × 10^-3) ÷ (8 × 10^5) = 0.3 × 10^-8. A = 0.3 is too small, so multiply A by 10 and subtract 1 from the power: 3 × 10^-9.
To find 'how many times larger' one quantity is than another, divide the larger by the smaller.
Writing the answer as a fraction first can help: 6.4 ÷ 1.6 = 4 and 10^7 ÷ 10^3 = 10^4.
core.p: To divide, **divide the A parts** and **subtract the powers of 10**: (A × 10^m) ÷ (B × 10^n) = (A ÷ B) × 10^(m-n). Be careful when subtracting a negative power, because subtracting a negative gives an addition. As with multiplication, the A part may need adjusting afterwards, which is especially common in division, where the A part can become less than 1.

bullets: Step 1: rewrite the number with the smaller power so that it has the same power as the larger one (this makes its A part smaller than 1).
Step 2: add or subtract the A parts.
Step 3: keep the common power and adjust to standard form if needed.
Example where the result needs adjusting: 8 × 10^6 + 5 × 10^6 = 13 × 10^6 = 1.3 × 10^7.
Never add the powers in addition: 10^4 + 10^4 is **not** 10^8; it is 2 × 10^4.
A calculator makes this easier if you enter numbers using the standard form key, but you must still write the answer correctly.
core.h: Adding and subtracting numbers in standard form
core.p: Adding and subtracting are different from multiplying and dividing: you **cannot** just add the A parts and the powers. Before adding or subtracting, both numbers must be written with the **same power of 10**, so that the digits line up in the same place values. Then add or subtract the A parts and keep the common power. Finally, convert back to standard form if needed. An alternative method is to convert both to ordinary numbers, calculate, and convert back.

bullets: Roots: the square root of 4 × 10^6 = 2 × 10^3, because the root of 10^6 is 10^3.
Roots with an even power: √(9 × 10^-4) = 3 × 10^-2. If the power is odd, rewrite first, for example 4 × 10^7 = 40 × 10^6, so the square root is about 6.32 × 10^3.
Check by converting to ordinary numbers: (3 × 10^4)^2 = 30 000² = 900 000 000 = 9 × 10^8.
core.h: Powers and roots of numbers in standard form
core.p: When you square, cube or take roots of a number in standard form, apply the power to **both** parts: the A part and the power of 10. The index law (10^m)^n = 10^(mn) means the powers of 10 are multiplied. After that, check whether the A part is still between 1 and 10 and adjust. These questions appear in physics formulae (for example, kinetic energy and areas) and in Higher tier algebraic contexts.

bullets: To enter 3.2 × 10^5, type 3.2, then the ×10^x or EXP key, then 5. Do **not** type 3.2 × 10 then ^ 5.
A display of 3.2E5 or 3.2 05 means 3.2 × 10^5. Write the answer in full, not with the E.
Check that a negative power is typed with the negative key (the (-) key, not subtract).
Always check the answer for sense: if you expect about 10^6 and see 10^12, you probably have mistyped.
If the calculator shows a very long decimal in a non-standard form, round to the required s.f. and convert to standard form.
Calculators can be switched to a scientific/standard form display mode, but you should still be able to do the manipulations by hand in non-calculator papers.
Brackets matter: use brackets around each standard form number when dividing, as in (6.4×10^7) ÷ (1.6×10^3).
core.h: Using a calculator with standard form
core.p: Calculators can enter, calculate with and display numbers in standard form, which is essential for non-calculator-sized values. You need to know your own calculator, but the common features are an **EXP** or **×10^x** key to enter the power of 10, and a display that may show a number such as 3.2E5 or 3.2 × 10^5 (depending on the model). The display is not the way to write your answer: you must always write it in proper standard form.

bullets: Time = distance ÷ speed. Light from the Sun: 1.5 × 10^8 km ÷ 3 × 10^5 km/s = 0.5 × 10^3 = 5 × 10^2 s = 500 s.
Unit conversions: 1 km = 10^3 m, 1 g = 10^-3 kg, 1 nm = 10^-9 m.
If you round 9.996 × 10^5 to 3 s.f., A rounds to 10.0, which is not allowed: write 1.00 × 10^6.
'How many times bigger' = divide, 'how many in total' = add, 'how many in a number of groups' = multiply.
Always put the **units** in the final answer and state the context sentence.
Estimates: round A to 1 s.f. and combine powers to check the size of the answer.
core.h: Solving problems in context, and rounding in standard form
core.p: Standard form problems usually involve a real-life context: speeds, populations, masses, distances, times, and costs. The key is to translate the question into a calculation, work in standard form, and give the answer in the form and accuracy that the question asks for. Remember that the A part is rounded to the stated number of **significant figures**, not decimal places; the power then does not change unless rounding pushes A up to 10.

bullets: Indices: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n), a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m-n), (a^m)^n = a^(mn), a^0 = 1, a^-n = 1/a^n.
Rounding and significant figures: standard form answers are normally given to 2 or 3 s.f.
Estimation: use 1 s.f. approximations in standard form to check calculations.
Compound measures: speed, density and pressure in science, often with large and small values.
Compound interest and growth: results may be written in standard form when numbers get large.
Higher tier extension: solve problems where numbers are given in mixed forms, such as 'How many times bigger is 2.4 × 10^8 than 6 × 10^5?' (answer 400 = 4 × 10^2).
Higher tier extension: simplify expressions like (4 × 10^6)^(1/2) or (8 × 10^-6)^(1/3) = 2 × 10^-2 using fractional indices.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher tier extension
core.p: Standard form is an application of the **laws of indices**, so it is closely linked to the Indices topics (integer, negative and fractional indices). It also supports estimation, significant figures, ratio and compound measures. Higher tier papers include questions where the numbers are given in words, in mixed form (such as 4 × 10^5 and 65 000), or in algebraic contexts such as 'x = 3 × 10^n, find n'. Be ready to convert, compare and calculate without being told which to do.

exam: Command words: 'Write ... in standard form' (1 mark), 'Work out ... Give your answer in standard form' (2 marks, with a method mark for the product or quotient of the A's and the powers), and 'Show that ...' (full working needed).
For a 2 mark conversion question, the mark scheme usually gives one mark for the correct digits in A and one for the correct power. If you write the power wrongly you can still earn the first mark.
In calculator questions write down the calculation you performed (for example 6.4 × 10^7 ÷ 1.6 × 10^3) as well as the answer.
Always give the answer in standard form if the question asks for it: an ordinary number loses the final mark.
In non-calculator questions, show the line before adjusting (e.g. 12.8 × 10^8) because the adjusting mark is often a separate mark.
For 'how many times bigger' questions divide, and write a sentence: 'The Earth is about 81 times heavier than the Moon'.
Check the sign of the power: big number → positive, small number → negative. A quick sense check often catches the most common error.
If a question says 'give your answer to 3 significant figures', round the A part and keep the power; if rounding makes A = 10.0, adjust to 1.00 × 10^(n+1).
Put units in context-based answers (m/s, kg, seconds, km).
In 4 and 5 mark problem-solving questions (for example, time for light to travel from the Sun), write the formula, substitute the values in standard form, calculate, then convert units if asked.
When ordering numbers, convert every number to standard form first and compare the power before the A part.

mistakes.r: A must be at least 1 and less than 10: 12.5 × 10^4 = 1.25 × 10^5.
A must be at least 1: 0.8 × 10^-3 = 8 × 10^-4 (multiply A by 10, subtract 1 from the power).
The point moves 3 places right to get 7.2, and the number is small, so 7.2 × 10^-3.
A negative power gives a small positive number: 5.2 × 10^-3 = 0.0052.
Add the powers when multiplying like bases: 10^3 × 10^4 = 10^7.

mistakes.w: (2 × 10^3)^2 = 4 × 10^5 (squaring only A, or doubling the power wrongly).

mistakes.r: Write it as 3.2 × 10^5; never copy the calculator display.
mistakes.w: Writing the answer as 3.2E5, or as 3.2 EXP 5, or 3.2^5.

summary: You must be able to write numbers in standard form A × 10^n (1 ≤ A < 10, n an integer), convert both ways between standard form and ordinary numbers, order numbers in standard form, and add, subtract, multiply, divide and take powers of them with and without a calculator. It matters because it is the language of very large and very small quantities in maths and science, and it is regularly tested in both calculator and non-calculator papers.

terms.d: A way of writing a number as A × 10^n, where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer.
The small raised number that tells you how many times the base is multiplied by itself.
The number that is raised to a power; in standard form the base is 10.
A whole number, which may be positive, negative or zero.
The size of a number measured by its power of 10, so that two numbers whose powers differ by 1 are one order of magnitude apart.
A power with a minus sign; 10^-n means 1 ÷ 10^n, giving a number smaller than 1.
1 divided by a number; for example the reciprocal of 10^3 is 10^-3.
The digits of a number counted from the first non-zero digit; used to round the A part of a standard form number.
The value of a digit given by its position in a number, for example tenths, hundreds or thousands.
The dot that separates the whole-number part from the fractional part of a number.
1 000 000 000 (one thousand million), which is 10^9 in standard form.
A number written in the usual decimal way, not in standard form.
The rules for combining powers: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n), a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m-n) and (a^m)^n = a^(mn).

worked.q: (a) Write 0.000 062 in standard form. (b) Write 3.5 × 10^4 as an ordinary number. (c) Write these in order, smallest first: 4.2 × 10^-2, 3.9 × 10^-2, 1.1 × 10^3, 9 × 10^-3. [4 marks]
steps: (a) First non-zero digit is 6. Move the point 5 places right to get 6.2. The number is small so n = -5.
(b) n = 4 so move the point 4 places right: 35 000.
(c) Compare powers first: -3 is smallest, then -2 (two numbers), then 3.

worked.q: The Sun is 1.5 × 10^8 km from the Earth. Light travels at 3 × 10^5 km/s. Work out how long light takes to reach the Earth from the Sun. Give your answer in seconds, in standard form, and then in minutes and seconds. [3 marks]
steps: Divide the A parts: 1.5 ÷ 3 = 0.5. Subtract the powers: 8 - 5 = 3. So 0.5 × 10^3.
A = 0.5 is too small: multiply by 10 and subtract 1 from the power: 5 × 10^2 seconds.
